<reason>Side B won by converting Side A's overtime-threshold defense into a concession trap: if the fifth shift stays but is billed at a premium, that is the 25% cost shock routed through a different line, and the carer still works five shifts. B then landed the sharpest analytical move of the debate — the historical analogies (eight-hour day, weekend) lacked the motion's operative "no reduction in base pay" clause, and priced genuinely marginal hours with pay free to adjust — which A never squarely answered. B also honestly and effectively answered A's best pressure question (what the warehouse picker ever gets) with the sectoral-bargaining/sequencing mechanism, and crystallized cleanly: the motion is redundant where slack exists and a wage-bill shock where it doesn't. A fought well — the "hidden cost paid in endurance" reframe, the default-flip mechanism, and the devastating "the sequence has a name for people at the back of it: never" line kept distributional justice live — and A's A1/A2 answers were direct and honest. But A's admission of "deliberately chosen higher public spending" and reliance on generational norm-drift left B's core objection standing: the motion's guaranteed effect is higher cost in the least affordable sectors, while its promised effect arrives only where the market already delivers it.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B's Rebuttal 1 [B2.1-B2.4]: seizing A's "simply pay overtime or hire" concession to show the cost shock survives unchanged, then dismantling the "job creation" answer by noting a vacancy is a post nobody applies for, not an unfilled desire to hire.</best_rebuttal>
